Ritu: Papa, I filled the form. Humanities, not commerce.
Ritu: I know you wanted me in the shop someday.
Vijay: I saw. Your mother told me.
Vijay: I typed three angry messages and deleted them.
Ritu: ok
Vijay put his phone down, then picked it up again.
Vijay: Not ok. I want to understand first. Why humanities?
Ritu: I want to study how cities grow. Maybe work on housing someday. I get excited about it, Papa. Not about ledgers.
Vijay: Your Dada started the shop with one tin trunk.
Vijay: I always thought you'd carry it forward.
Ritu: I can still love the shop. I just don't want to run it.
Vijay: That's hard to hear.
Vijay: But you just explained yourself better than I could at sixteen, beti.
Vijay: Come down for dinner. Tell me about these cities.
Ritu: 🙂 coming

qa.q: What subject did Ritu choose on the form?
What was Vijay feeling when he typed and deleted three angry messages?
qa.a: He felt angry and afraid of losing his hope that Ritu would carry the shop forward, but he held back to understand first.

qa.q: What choice did Vijay make that kept the chat from turning into a fight?
qa.a: He asked 'Why humanities?' before reacting, and then invited Ritu down to dinner to hear more.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when her father says she explained herself better than he could at sixteen?
qa.a: Ritu might feel relieved and respected, since her father listened and even admired how clearly she gave her reasons.

grounding: Shows a father facing his teenage daughter's unexpected career choice with anger, grief and pride, and listening to her reasons before responding.

subtype: Parent facing the child's different values [Receiver]
passage:
At the Thursday cattle market outside the kasba, Wasim sold three goats before noon and felt nothing. Last night his son Faiz, fifteen, had pushed away the mutton curry and said quietly, 'Abbu, I don't want to eat meat anymore. And I don't want to trade goats.'
Wasim had walked out without a word.
On the bus home he sat beside Mahima, the schoolteacher from the next lane. 'Three generations,' he said. 'And he looks at our work like it's wrong.'
'Did you ask him why?'
He hadn't.
That evening he found Faiz feeding the young goat by the shed. Wasim sat on an upturned bucket. 'Tell me. From the start. I'll listen first.'
Faiz talked for a long time, about the goats' faces, about a veterinary course in the city. Wasim felt fear in his chest, and a strange pride too, at how carefully his boy had thought.

qa.q: What did Faiz push away at dinner?
What mixed feelings did Wasim have while Faiz talked by the shed?
qa.a: He felt fear in his chest and also a strange pride at how carefully his son had thought it through.

qa.q: What turning point sent Wasim back to talk with Faiz?
qa.a: Mahima's question 'Did you ask him why?' made him see he hadn't, so he chose to sit down and listen first.

qa.q: How might Faiz have felt when his father walked out without a word?
qa.a: Faiz may have felt rejected and worried that his father saw the choice as an insult to three generations of family work.

grounding: Shows a father whose teenage son chooses values and a path he did not expect, feeling fear and pride, and choosing to listen before responding.
